conceptTag: The cost of too many products
readerTitle: Why P&G chose to sell fewer brands
caseNote: 실제 기업 (P&G, 2014년 브랜드 정리 발표) + 가상 사례 (식당 메뉴, 소프트웨어 요금제)
insight: 제품 하나의 비용은 그 제품 장부에 다 잡히지 않는다. 품목 수가 늘수록 공용 비용이 조용히 커진다.
misconception: 팔리는 만큼 이익이 나는 제품이라면 많을수록 좋다. 매출이 작은 제품을 빼면 그만큼 이익도 준다.

sources.text: Procter & Gamble, fiscal Q4 2014 earnings call and press coverage (August 2014): plan to keep 70–80 core brands and exit up to 100 brands
복잡성 비용(complexity cost)과 품목 수 관리에 관한 운영관리 일반 개념
식당과 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: P&G 2014년 8월 발표 내용 확인 필요: 유지할 브랜드 70~80개, 매각·정리 대상 최대 약 90~100개, 유지 브랜드가 매출 약 90%, 이익 95% 이상 차지. 카드에는 "up to 100", "about 90% of sales", "more than 95% of profit"으로 적었습니다.
A.G. Lafley의 "less will be much more" 발언은 널리 보도되었으나 원문 확인 전이라 카드에 직접 인용하지 않았습니다.
정리 이후 P&G의 실적 변화는 다른 요인이 많아 인과를 단정하기 어렵습니다. 카드에서 결과를 주장하지 않았습니다.
식당 예시(메뉴 60개 → 25개)와 소프트웨어 요금제 예시는 가상이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why P&G chose to sell fewer brands
body: In August 2014, Procter & Gamble, one of the world's biggest consumer goods companies, made an unusual announcement.
It would keep 70 to 80 brands and sell or close **up to 100** others. Many of those brands were still selling. Some were profitable on their own.

image.label: A crowded shelf being thinned to a few products
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 가득 찬 마트 진열대에서 손이 여러 상품을 걷어내고, 남은 몇 개 상품이 더 크고 선명하게 보임. 실제 브랜드 로고나 포장 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Cut the small brands?
body: Imagine you run a large household goods company. Your smallest brands together bring in about 10% of sales. Each one shows a modest profit in its own report.
If you drop them all, what most likely happens to total profit?

options.text: It falls by about 10%, in line with sales
options.feedback: This assumes each brand's report shows all its costs. Often it doesn't, so the true loss is smaller than the sales figure suggests.

options.text: It falls a little at first, then can hold or even rise
options.feedback: Small brands share factories, sales teams and management time. Removing them frees those costs, though some savings take time to show up.

options.text: It doesn't matter. Any brand with a profit should stay
options.feedback: True if the profit figure is complete. The question is what that figure leaves out.

cards.title: 10% of sales, under 5% of profit.
body: According to P&G, the 70 to 80 brands it kept made about **90% of sales** and more than **95% of profit**.
So the brands it planned to exit brought in about a tenth of sales but less than a twentieth of profit. And they still needed factories, shelf space, marketing plans and managers' attention.
The company's view was simple: a shorter list would let it focus people and money on the brands that carried the business.

cards.title: Complexity cost
body: **Complexity cost** is the cost of having many products, not of making many units. It grows with the number of items you offer, even if total sales stay the same.
Each new item looks cheap on its own. The cost hides in shared places: planning, storage, training, mistakes and time spent switching from one item to another.

image.label: Costs rising with the number of items, not the volume
image.brief: 두 그래프 나란히. 왼쪽: 같은 판매량, 품목 5개 → 공용 비용 막대 낮음. 오른쪽: 같은 판매량, 품목 20개 → 공용 비용 막대 높음. 라벨 "Same sales", "More items", "Shared costs".

cards.title: Where the extra cost goes.
body: Every item you add brings work that rarely shows in its own numbers:
list: **Forecasting and stock:** more items to predict, more chances to run out or overbuy
**Changeovers:** time lost switching machines, recipes or setups
**Training and errors:** more to learn, more to get wrong
cards.callout: These costs sit in shared overhead, so small products look more profitable than they are.

cards.title: A menu with 60 dishes.
body: A family restaurant offers 60 dishes. Ten of them make most of the orders. The other 50 still need their own ingredients in the fridge, their own prep and their own place in the cooks' memory.
Rarely ordered dishes mean ingredients that spoil before they're used. A long menu also slows the kitchen at the busiest hour.
Cut to 25 dishes, and the kitchen can stock less, waste less and cook faster, often with the same number of guests.

image.label: A long menu shrinking to a short one
image.brief: 긴 두루마리 메뉴판이 짧은 한 장짜리 메뉴판으로 바뀌는 모습. 뒤쪽 주방에서 냉장고 속 재료 통이 줄어들고 요리사가 여유로워 보임.

cards.title: Small sellers aren't always dead weight.
body: Some low-volume items do a job the sales report misses. A kids' meal brings in whole families. A rare spare part keeps a big customer loyal. A niche flavor may be the reason some shoppers visit at all.
Before cutting, ask who buys the item and what else they buy. And cut in steps: watch what customers do after each change, not just what the spreadsheet predicted.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your software product has grown to nine pricing plans, plus a few old ones that early users still keep. Support often has to check which plan a user is on before answering. Every new feature must be set up for each plan.

options.text: Add a tenth plan for a segment asking for one
options.feedback: You might win that segment, but every feature, bill and support ticket gets a little harder again.

options.text: Merge into three or four plans, and move old plans over with a clear notice and a fair price
options.feedback: You cut work in billing, support and product. The cost is some upset users, which a careful move and notice can soften.

options.text: Hide the old plans from the website but keep running them
options.feedback: It simplifies what new users see, but the hidden work inside the company stays the same.

cards.title: Every product you add costs more than its own report shows.
body: Judge your range by what the whole business carries, not by each item's sales alone.
**Try it today:** list your products from best to worst seller. Look at the bottom fifth. For each one, write who buys it and what work it adds.
